title: Introduction: The Illusion of a Finished Portfolio Dashboard - Morning 1: Zero-Price Fallbacks & JavaScript "OR" Truthiness - Morning 2: Handling Unheld Stocks & Rejecting Incomplete Payloads
text: Here's a portfolio dashboard the way its reader sees it over morning coffee. Five stocks, one total $65,98 up 21%. It looks finished, but every number on this screen arrived through a few quiet handoffs, places where one part of the system takes another part's word for it. So, let's spend four mornings with this dashboard and on each one let one of those handoffs slip. Hi, this is Tanme Kolc Carney in for humanitarians AI. This week, I contributed to Microoft, which is both a book and a working repository for finance pipelines. It calls them recipes. Two of them sit behind this dashboard. One fetches the prices and does the math. The other calls it and draws the screen. My pull request now merged added checks to both and rebuilt the math step so it runs on test data. Every price you'll see is invented for testing. Morning one. Vote for one stock comes back with a price of zero. The

Workflow reads the price with a JavaScript or and a JavaScript zero counts as missing. So it quietly uses the previous close 590 and the dashboard looks perfectly normal. The math is right. The reader just doesn't know which price they're looking at. I kept that behavior exactly because it's the workflow's choice, not mine. And the recipe now notes it for the maintainers. What changed is the record. For every stock, it now says which price was used. Morning two. A response comes back for a symbol the portfolio doesn't hold. In the original, the calculation looks up how many shares you own, finds nothing, and stops with an error. Now, the check before it catches the response first and sets it aside with a reason. And the calculation refuses to run on anything that check turned away. Nothing half-finish reaches the screen. Warning three. And this one surprised me. Out twice inside the same workflow. One copy decides which prices to fetch. The other one does the math. Edit the shares in the first and the math keeps using the second. The total doesn't move and nothing says why. So the first step now reads both copies and stops if they disagree naming the difference. Mo four. The dashboard doesn't hold any prices itself. It calls the price workflow and it finds it by name. The ID that would pin it down is still a placeholder. So, the dashboard's first step now checks that the name it calls is the price workflow's real name and stops if it isn't. And then there was the morning it was my own check. To make sure these checks could actually fail, I broke my own calculation on purpose and ran the test that's meant to catch it. It passed all green, but the broken version had never run at all.
